candidates.speaker: Joel Settecase
candidates.proposition: Christian theism uniquely supplies the preconditions required for logic, knowledge, and intelligible reasoning.
candidates.attributionBasis: The turn begins with Joel's explicit statement of Christian belief and continues uninterrupted until Tom responds.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This is Joel's foundational case for the motion and establishes the transcendental explanatory claim contested throughout the exchange.
candidates.contextSummary: After introductory remarks, Joel presents Christian revelation as the necessary basis of intelligibility and briefly identifies experience, scripture, morality, science, and prophecy as supporting considerations.

candidates.speaker: Tom Jump
candidates.proposition: Direct experience requires no presuppositions, while logic and mathematics can be constructed as formal descriptions whose truths do not depend on God.
candidates.attributionBasis: Tom explicitly introduces the intelligibility objection and speaks continuously until Joel attempts to interject.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This directly denies the necessity claim at the center of Joel's case and offers a naturalistic account of logical and mathematical intelligibility.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Joel's claim that Christian theism is the only possible explanation for intelligibility and knowledge.

candidates.contextSummary: Tom answers Joel's opening case by treating experience as epistemically prior and logic and mathematics as formal languages that remain necessarily applicable regardless of whether God exists.

candidates.speaker: Tom Jump
candidates.proposition: The historical origin of mathematical language is irrelevant to whether logic and mathematics require God, because their necessity holds under any possible reality.
candidates.attributionBasis: Tom explicitly returns to his principal argument after rebutting Joel's questions about the historical invention of mathematics.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The move redirects an extended historical dispute back to the decisive modal claim that intelligibility remains available without divine presupposition.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Joel's challenge that Tom had not substantiated the human invention of mathematics or identified its inventors.

candidates.contextSummary: Following disagreement about mathematical history and evidential burdens, Tom restates that identity and arithmetic cannot become false in a godless reality and places the contrary burden on Joel.

candidates.speaker: Joel Settecase
candidates.proposition: Tom's account appears to require an unexplained correspondence between mathematical concepts in his mind and reality beyond his mind.
candidates.attributionBasis: Joel asks a focused challenge in his own turn immediately after Tom claims that mathematics works without presupposing an external world.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The challenge targets the bridge from private cognition to objective necessity, which becomes Joel's principal criticism of Tom's alternative account.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Tom's assertion that mathematics and logic work regardless of whether reality is external, idealist, or solipsistic.

candidates.contextSummary: After Tom distinguishes mathematical language from whatever internal or external reality it describes, Joel presses whether the account covertly assumes mind-world correspondence.

candidates.speaker: Tom Jump
candidates.proposition: The impossibility of mistakenly believing that one exists supplies a self-validating basis from which logic and mathematics apply normatively to every thinker and object.
candidates.attributionBasis: Tom develops this derivation across several clarifying exchanges, with his substantive answers clearly attributable despite brief questions from Joel.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This provides Tom's core epistemic foundation for intelligibility without God and attempts to connect first-person certainty to universally applicable logical structure.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Joel's objection that Tom was extrapolating from mathematical ideas in his own mind to all minds and all reality.

candidates.contextSummary: Tom identifies certainty of his own existence as prior to logic and mathematics, then argues that the same principle applies to thinking beings, individual objects, and their plurality.

candidates.speaker: Joel Settecase
candidates.proposition: Tom illegitimately leaps from self-authenticating first-person experience to principles claimed as necessarily descriptive and normative for all reality.
candidates.attributionBasis: Joel addresses the audience and gives an extended characterization of Tom's reasoning before Tom begins his rebuttal.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This articulates Joel's main internal critique of Tom's proposed foundation by denying that personal certainty warrants universal logical and mathematical conclusions.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Tom's derivation of universally normative logic and mathematics from the certainty that he cannot mistakenly believe he exists.

candidates.contextSummary: Joel summarizes Tom's position as beginning with incorrigible first-person awareness and argues that an additional inferential leap is needed to reach necessary truths governing reality as a whole.

candidates.speaker: Tom Jump
candidates.proposition: The certainty of one's existence is true in every possible reality, so it is not merely an internal mental fact and does not depend on God.
candidates.attributionBasis: Tom explicitly corrects Joel's characterization and completes the correction after a brief acknowledgment allowing him to continue.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This defends the modal reach of Tom's foundational certainty against Joel's accusation that it remains confined to subjective cognition.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Joel's characterization of Tom's foundation as consisting only of conceptions located within Tom's own mind.

candidates.contextSummary: Amid interruptions, Tom distinguishes the epistemic starting point from its modal status and maintains that no external, internal, idealist, materialist, theistic, or atheistic reality could falsify the certainty.

candidates.speaker: Joel Settecase
candidates.proposition: Tom has not identified a connective principle that licenses conclusions about every possible world from facts about his own believing and thinking.
candidates.attributionBasis: Joel states the objection as a sustained series of questions directed specifically at the bridge in Tom's reasoning.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The move isolates the disputed inference between epistemic certainty and modal universality rather than merely repeating a general request for justification.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Tom's claim that his inability to believe he exists and be wrong establishes what must hold across all possible worlds.

candidates.contextSummary: Joel asks whether the proposed connecting principle originates within Tom's mind or exists necessarily apart from it, sharpening the dispute over subjective access and objective modality.

candidates.speaker: Tom Jump
candidates.proposition: Logical propositions are mind-dependent sentences, whereas the reality they describe is objective; their descriptive success does not require transcendent propositions.
candidates.attributionBasis: Tom gives a continuous analogy between logical expressions and ordinary words in direct response to Joel's proposed mind-independent propositions.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This supplies Tom's semantic alternative to Joel's apparent argument for necessarily existing mental entities and preserves objective reality without divine propositions.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Joel's suggestion that true logical propositions must exist necessarily and independently of every human mind.

candidates.contextSummary: Tom distinguishes linguistic representations from their referents, using an ordinary-word analogy to argue that identity statements exist as sentences in minds while objectively describing reality.

candidates.speaker: Tom Jump
candidates.proposition: Reality cannot cease to be reality under any condition, including temporal change, so logical identity necessarily holds throughout past and future time.
candidates.attributionBasis: Tom begins the answer inside the owned core and completes the stated premises and conclusion in the delivered lookahead before Joel acknowledges it.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The move extends Tom's necessity argument across time and provides the explicit missing-premise structure Joel repeatedly requested near the core boundary.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Joel's demand for the missing premise connecting Tom's self-existence argument to the future persistence of logical laws.

candidates.contextSummary: Tom analogizes personal identity with reality's self-identity, then formulates the temporal argument by asserting that nothing, including time or change, can make reality cease being reality.
